title: Scaling
tagline: Scaling laws, compute budgets, parallelism, low-precision training and hardware
summary: Language models improve predictably with scale. This course studies empirical scaling laws and compute-optimal training, estimates the FLOPs and memory of training runs, and explains how data, tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism, sharded optimisers and low-precision arithmetic spread training across thousands of accelerators.
overview: One of the most consequential empirical findings about language models is that their loss falls smoothly and predictably as parameters, data and compute grow. Scaling laws turned model building into a planning problem — how big a model, how many tokens, how much compute — and acting on the answers requires training runs on thousands of accelerators for weeks or months. This course covers both halves: the empirical science of scaling, and the systems engineering that makes very large training runs possible.

The first chapters fit and interpret scaling laws and derive compute-optimal allocations in the style of Chinchilla, including why practitioners now deliberately train smaller models for longer to make inference cheaper. The arithmetic of a training step — about six floating-point operations per parameter per token, plus activation and optimiser memory — gives the budget, and the accelerator chapters explain what limits throughput: memory bandwidth, arithmetic intensity and the roofline model. Low-precision formats such as bf16 and fp8 stretch the hardware further. Parallelism then spreads the work: data parallelism with all-reduce, sharded optimisers (ZeRO, FSDP), tensor and pipeline parallelism, and expert parallelism for mixtures of experts. The last chapter covers the engineering of the largest runs: networks, failures, checkpointing and monitoring.

Scaling laws are empirical regularities fitted over limited ranges, not laws of nature, and their exponents depend on data, architecture and how they were measured. Practise the back-of-the-envelope estimates until they are automatic — FLOPs, memory per device, time per step — because they decide whether a plan is feasible before any code runs.
outcomes: Fit power laws relating loss to parameters, data and compute, and judge the range over which they hold.
Derive compute-optimal model and data sizes, and explain when to train smaller models for longer.
Estimate the FLOPs, memory and wall-clock time of a training run.
Analyse accelerator performance with arithmetic intensity and the roofline model.
Explain floating-point formats and the practice of bf16 and fp8 training.
Compare data, tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism and sharded optimisers, and combine them for a given model and cluster.
Describe the engineering of large training runs: networking, fault tolerance and checkpointing.

history.title: Deep learning scaling is predictable
history.detail: Hestness and colleagues at Baidu measured power-law relations between training-set size and error across translation, language modelling, image classification and speech recognition.

history.title: Mixed-precision training
history.detail: Micikevicius and colleagues trained networks in 16-bit floating point with a 32-bit master copy of the weights and loss scaling, nearly halving memory without losing accuracy.

history.title: GPipe
history.detail: Huang and colleagues split a model into stages on different devices and kept them busy by pipelining micro-batches through them.

history.title: Megatron-LM
history.detail: Shoeybi and colleagues at NVIDIA split the matrices of each Transformer layer across GPUs — the tensor parallelism used to train most large models.

history.title: ZeRO
history.detail: Rajbhandari and colleagues at Microsoft sharded optimiser states, gradients and parameters across data-parallel workers, removing the memory redundancy of data parallelism.

history.title: Scaling laws for neural language models
history.detail: Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI found that language-model loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute over many orders of magnitude.

history.title: Chinchilla
history.detail: Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind showed that large models had been undertrained: for a fixed compute budget, parameters and training tokens should grow in proportion — roughly twenty tokens per parameter.

history.title: Training on sixteen thousand GPUs
history.detail: Meta’s Llama 3 report described training a 405-billion-parameter model on up to 16,000 H100 GPUs, including how often hardware failures interrupted the run.
